bodyHtml:
What is an inspection data management system (IDMS)?

An inspection data management system, or IDMS, is the place where inspection results and the evidence behind them are stored as structured, searchable records instead of loose files. It holds the reports, the readings, the photos, the technician certificates and the calibration records, linked to each other and to the job, so anyone reviewing the data later can see what was found, how it was found and whether the finding can be trusted.

Most inspection data in North America still lives in a mix of PDFs on a shared drive, Excel workbooks, email attachments and paper travellers in a filing cabinet. That works until someone needs to answer a question across many jobs: every PAUT report on a given client's welds this year, every report signed by a technician whose cert has since been revoked, or every job where a specific UT instrument was used before it failed calibration. A folder structure cannot answer those questions. A structured IDMS can.

This section explains what an IDMS should hold, how inspection data should be structured, what retention and audit trails look like, and how the Atlantis ERP solution and Atlantis Digital Twins store and present inspection data for NDT and inspection companies.

IDMS vs inspection management software vs a document folder

An IDMS is about the data; inspection management software is about the work. In a good setup, they are the same system, because the data is captured while the work is being managed.

ApproachWhat it storesWhat it cannot tell you
Shared drive or document folderFinal PDFs and spreadsheetsWhich instrument, cert or procedure revision sits behind each result, without opening every file
Stand-alone reporting toolReport data and templatesWhether the technician was certified or the instrument calibrated on the day
Inspection data management inside the Atlantis ERPStructured report data, photos, signatures, certificates, calibration records, procedures, linked to the jobEngineering conclusions about the asset, which remain with the owner's integrity team

The point of that last column is honesty about scope: an IDMS makes the data reliable and findable. It does not replace the engineer who decides what the data means for the asset.

Inspection data management: how the data should be structured

Good inspection data management starts with deciding what is a field and what is an attachment. Anything you will ever filter, sort or report on should be a field. Anything that is evidence for a human reader, such as a scanned certificate or a site photo, can be an attachment, but it should be attached to the right record.

Data typeWhat to capture as structured dataWhere it lives in Atlantis
Report headerMethod, report number, client, site, work order, request, WPS, contract, drawing numbers, procedure and standard referencesNDT Reports
Method dataUT probe calibration table; RT source, technique, IQI type and placement; MT technique and particles; PT method and developer; PAUT focal laws; MFL scan mode; UT thickness readings by directionNDT Reports, per method
FindingsWeld or job lines with defect type and orientation; overall resultNDT Reports
Photos and signaturesCaptured in the field against the reportOffline field app, synced to the report
PeopleScheme, level, method, dates, OJT and training hours, vision testsCertificates
EquipmentSerial, type, firmware, condition, calibration results and due datesAsset Management
ProceduresDocument number, revision, method, scope, standard, acceptance criteriaProcedures

Reports as structured records, not just PDFs

The core of any IDMS is the inspection report, and the key design choice is that the report is a record first and a PDF second. In the Atlantis ERP there are 17 report types: UT, RT, MT, PT, VT, ECT, IRIS, PAUT, MFL, TOFD, PWHT, PMI, hardness, UT thickness, ferrite, holiday/coating and computed radiography. Each has its own numbering sequence, so a report number tells you the method at a glance and numbering gaps are easy to spot.

Each type holds the fields that method actually needs. A UT report is not a generic form with a comments box; it carries the probe calibration table. An RT report records source, technique, IQI type and placement. A PAUT report records focal laws. UT thickness readings are held by direction, and weld and job lines hold defect type and orientation. The overall result is one of three explicit values: acceptable, not acceptable, or acceptable with remarks, which makes it possible to filter for every rejectable finding on a project.

The PDF is then generated from that record on your versioned company template, in Excel, Word, PDF or HTML, with logo, header and footer. If a client requires their own Excel sheet, fields are mapped to cells and the sheet fills automatically. Because the template is versioned, you can tell which layout a historical report was issued on.

Readings, photos and field attachments

Field data is where inspection data management usually breaks down, because it is captured in the worst conditions: no signal, gloves on, time pressure. If capture is awkward, data ends up on paper and gets retyped later, and every retype is a chance for a transposed reading.

The Atlantis field app is an installable web app that works without signal. Drafts and photos are stored locally on the device and synced when coverage returns. The technician picks the method, captures photos, signs on screen and previews the PDF before submitting. Through the REST API for field devices, the app knows which jobs are assigned to the technician and which equipment has been issued to them, so readings are recorded against the right job and instrument from the start.

Photos are stored against the report rather than in a separate camera roll. In marine mode, inspection photos are laid out two to a row in the output PDF, alongside a vessel cover page and photo and the inspection location and dates. For instrument output files or scans your process needs to keep, the attachment handling is configured during implementation so they land on the correct report.

Certificates and calibration records linked to the data

An inspection result is only as credible as the person and the instrument that produced it. An IDMS should therefore link each result to the qualification and calibration evidence, not store them in separate silos.

In the Atlantis ERP, technician certifications record scheme (SNT-TC-1A, CP-189, ISO 9712, PCN, CSWIP or other), level, method, certifying body, issue, expiry and renewal dates, OJT hours, training hours, exam results and attachments. Status is computed automatically as active, expiring soon, expired or revoked. Vision tests record near vision (Jaeger J1/J2), far vision, colour perception and contrast with examiner, clinic, certificate file and expiry. Examination sheets hold general, specific and practical scores.

Instrument calibration records hold provider, certificate number, standard, range, uncertainty, accredited-lab flag, result (pass, fail or conditional) and next due date, and the calibration certificate register keeps the PDF with the lab's accreditation number and a valid, expiring or expired status. Because instruments are tracked by serial and issued to technicians through an approved issue and return workflow, you can connect a report to the serial that was on site. For marine reports, the output PDF merges the class certificate, the inspector's Level II certificate and the calibration certificate into one file.

Retention and audit trails

Retention and audit trails answer two questions: how long do we keep inspection data, and can we show that nobody changed it after sign-off? The first depends on you; the second depends on the system.

Retention periods are driven by your client contracts, the construction or inspection code the work was done to, your quality management system and, in some sectors, regulators. Because those differ from job to job, retention rules are configured during implementation rather than hard-coded, and records are kept in the system rather than on individual laptops.

For audit trails, the Atlantis ERP records the path each item took:

  • Reports move through draft, in progress, review, approved and sent, with inspector, reviewer and approver signatures, and a third-party or authorized inspector name and signature where required.
  • Procedures move through draft, submitted, reviewed, approved and published; approved revisions are locked, rejections carry a reason, and a snapshot of every revision is kept.
  • Equipment issue and return runs through supervisor and manager approval with condition recorded both ways; inbound and outbound movements and the maintenance log are kept against the serial.
  • Dispatch records who was assigned, where and when, through planned, dispatched, in field, submitted and closed.
  • Timesheets are approved and flag technicians whose certificate was not valid.

If you need to understand how your existing records would map into this structure, send us a sample of your current reports and registers.

How the Atlantis ERP stores inspection data

In the Atlantis ERP, inspection data is stored around the job. A project carries client PO, contract, methods, codes, scope and acceptance criteria. Project tasks carry method, technician, component, result, indication and defect counts, and procedure and WPS references. The team assignment carries site coordinates, dates, technicians and equipment serials. Reports sit against the job with their method data, photos and signatures.

Around the job sit the reference registers: certificates for people, calibration and maintenance for equipment, the procedure register, and company certifications such as ISO accreditations with alert days. Dashboards summarise the live state: equipment calibration due or overdue, certificates expiring or expired, and issued equipment overdue for return.

Because the commercial apps are in the same system, a report can be traced to the quote and invoice for the job, which helps when a client disputes whether an item was inspected or billed. The system is affordable, accessible and fully customizable, and is configured for your methods, templates and registers during implementation.

How Atlantis Digital Twins presents inspection data

Stored data is only useful if people can read it. For owner-operators and asset managers, tables of readings across hundreds of components are hard to interpret. Atlantis Digital Twins presents inspection data on a 3D model of the asset: damage and indication mapping shows where findings sit on the equipment, and thickness and remaining-life trends show how readings have moved between inspections.

The Digital Twin Reporting Software ties inspection reports to that 3D view, so a reviewer can open the report from the location on the model rather than hunting through a folder. This is useful at refineries, petrochemical plants, tank terminals and power stations, where the same equipment is inspected across several turnarounds and the story is in the trend.

The boundary matters. The Digital Twin visualises the data and the trends; it does not make integrity decisions. Owner-operators' integrity engineers carry out their own assessments of damage, remaining life and next inspection dates using the methodologies and tools they have chosen. The Atlantis ERP does not calculate inspection intervals, and it does not hold a thickness monitoring location database; it records the inspection reports and readings that feed the owner's own process.

Getting inspection data in and out: open REST API

An IDMS that locks data in is a liability. The Atlantis ERP has an open REST API and integrates with SAP, Maximo, NetSuite, QuickBooks or any system that accepts API connections, with the scope agreed per implementation.

For contractors, typical flows are receiving work orders from a client's maintenance system so the job and report carry the client's reference, and returning approved report files or report status when a job closes. For owner-operators, the flow is often the reverse: pulling approved contractor reports into their own asset records. On the field side, the API already handles jobs assigned to a technician, equipment issued to them, report submission and sync.

Exports for audits or client handover, such as report registers, certificate registers and calibration lists, are configured during implementation to match the formats your clients and auditors ask for.

Migrating from shared drives and spreadsheets

Most companies moving to an inspection data management system start with years of history in folders. A practical migration does not try to convert every old PDF into structured data. It loads the live registers first, which are current technicians and certifications, current instruments with serials and calibration due dates, and the current procedure register, and then starts new reports in the structured format.

Historical reports can be attached to the relevant client and job records so they are findable, while new work builds a clean structured history from day one. Report templates are rebuilt so the output looks like what your clients already accept, which avoids a round of client re-approval of your report format. For small NDT companies this is usually a short project; larger contractors with many templates and integrations take longer, and we scope it up front.

To plan a migration for your own records, talk to us about what you have today.

Frequently asked questions

What does IDMS stand for?

IDMS stands for inspection data management system: a system that stores inspection reports, readings, photos, certificates and calibration records as linked, searchable records rather than loose files.

What data should an inspection data management system hold?

At minimum: structured report data by method, findings and results, photos and signatures, procedure and standard references, technician certifications and vision tests, and instrument calibration records, all linked to the job.

How does the Atlantis ERP keep an audit trail?

Reports and procedures move through defined workflows with named, signed reviewers and approvers. Approved procedure revisions are locked with snapshots kept, and equipment issue and return is approved and logged with condition.

Does the system calculate remaining life or inspection intervals?

No. Atlantis Digital Twins visualises thickness and remaining-life trends from inspection data, but interval and integrity decisions are made by the owner-operator's own engineers and tools. The ERP does not calculate inspection intervals.

Can we keep our existing report formats?

Yes. Versioned company templates in Excel, Word, PDF or HTML are supported, and Excel templates fill automatically from mapped fields.

Can inspection data be sent to SAP or Maximo?

Yes, through the open REST API, which integrates with SAP, Maximo, NetSuite, QuickBooks or any system that accepts API connections, scoped per implementation.

How is an IDMS from Atlantis priced?

Quote on request, depending on the apps, templates and integrations you need. Request a quote and demo.
